newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti PC workers fear for future.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti PC workers fear for future.

text.p: The sudden exit of Carlo De Benedetti from the board of hi-tech group Olivetti this week has plunged the future of its personal computer company and the sector's 2,000 workers into uncertainty.
Personal computers have gone from being Olivetti's 1980s success story to its Achille's heel of the 1990s as hard-hitting competition and tough economic conditions sent it into the red.

De Benedetti, who built Olivetti into an information technology company from an ailing typewriter producer, promised trade unions in the last restructuring round almost a year ago that the personal computer division would not be dismantled.

His departure means union leaders no longer count on that promise and, fearing for jobs at Olivetti's headquarters in the small north western town of Ivrea, they say the group's case is a national one in which the government should intervene.
"What we are afraid of is that the new management will decide to abandon the less profitable sector of Olivetti," said Luigi Angeletti, leader of the Uilm metalworkers' union.

"If the PC division shuts down, not only the 2,000 workers involved will be without a job but also another couple of thousand people whose earnings depend on it would be hit," said Claudio Sabattini, leader of one of Italy's largest engineering unions the Fiom.

Olivetti said on Tuesday after De Benedetti quit that it had made 200 billion lire ($132 milion) of provisions for divestments and restructuring deriving from its decision "to accelerate the reduction of its presence in the hardware sector".

This was widely taken at the time to mean Olivetti wanted to leave the personal computer field but since then there has been little clarity over exactly what is planned. Chief executive Francesco Caio, talking to equity analysts on Wednesday, gave no hint the PC unit was up for immediate sale or closure.
The personal computer company lost 200 billion lire ($132.5 million) in 1995 and 10 billion lire in the first half of 1996 on 991.5 billion lire of revenue.

Worried about the future of 4,000 Italian families whose income is tied to the group, leaders of the three main engineering unions Fiom, Fim and Uilm have asked for a meeting with Caio and De Benedetti's successor Antonio Tesone. Workers staged a spontaneous stoppage on Wednesday at Olivetti's industrial site in Ivrea and further action is likely.
Guglielmo Epifani, joint secretary of the CGIL trade union, expressed deep concern at De Benedetti's departure, saying it was a pointer to the difficulties the group faces.
Olivetti has failed to break even since 1990 and made a further pre-tax loss for the first half of 1996 of 440.2 billion lire after a full year loss of 1.598 trillion in 1995.
Epifani said abandoning information technology and focusing entirely on telecommunications would be a mistake for Olivetti and called the IT sector strategic for the future.

"It wouldn't make sense - when we've done a lot to get the government to set up an agency to computerise public administration - to have a strategic sector in which there is no domestic production base," he said.

Leaders of Italy's biggest trade union confederations were expected to discuss Olivetti at a meeting on employment with Industry Minister PierLuigi Bersani later on Thursday which was scheduled before De Benedetti resigned. Bersani will then meet metal and engineering union leaders in nine days' time.
Sabattini said the government could create an information and technology group by merging Olivetti and software company Finsiel, which is part of state telecomunications holding Stet.
"The ownership could be private or public...the point is Olivetti cannot be left on its own," Sabattini said.
